contributions.headingText: Paget disease of the vulva is an in situ adenocarcinoma of the vulvar skin, with or without underlying invasive adenocarcinoma. Secondary involvement of vulvar skin by carcinoma of rectal, bladder, or cervical origin is designated “secondary Paget disease”.
Acceptable: extramammary Paget disease; primary vulvar Paget disease
Vulvar Paget disease can arise from either the labium minus or the labium majus and can extend onto extravulvar skin and/or involve the vaginal or (rarely) cervical mucosa.
Patients present with a pruritic, erythematous, eczematous lesion mimicking a vulvar dermatosis or high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion (VIN 3).
Primary vulvar Paget disease is uncommon, typically affecting white women aged > 60 years {26971063}.

Vulvar Paget disease is thought to originate from a pluripotent stem cell in the epidermis or skin adnexa. Paget cells can express breast cancer biomarkers. Most express ER and PR; ERBB2 (HER2) expression is less common, and the reported frequency of ERBB2 (HER2) amplification varies {15272283; 17701193; 28418164; 31297606}. Mutations in genes encoding the PI3K/AKT cascade have been found to significantly correlate with CDH1 hypermethylation {22821211; 28291131}. A study using comparative genomic hybridization revealed amplification at chromosomes Xcent-q21 and 19, as well as loss at 10q24-qter {16086738}.
Paget disease is typically slightly raised and reddened compared with adjacent normal skin, with ill-defined margins.

Large round Paget cells with pale cytoplasm and a large nucleus, frequently with a prominent nucleolus, are present within the epidermis; these are predominantly located in the basal layers of the epidermis, sometimes with extension of isolated cells or small nests of cells upwards through the superficial layers of the epidermis. Involvement of the epithelium of skin adnexa is common. The cytoplasm contains mucin, demonstrable with PAS or mucicarmine stains, in most cases. A prominent host inflammatory response in the superficial dermis is common, with prominent neovascularization; this correlates with the eczematous clinical appearance. Dermal invasion is usually in the form of individual or small groups of cells, sometimes forming glandular structures.

The cells of primary Paget disease consistently express CK7, which serves to distinguish them from the cells of high-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion, HPV-independent VIN, and melanoma {10542944}. CK7 staining may assist in identifying small foci of dermal invasion. EMA, CAM5.2, CEA, and GATA3 are typically diffusely positive. Melanoma markers and HPV are negative, but p16 may be diffusely positive {23370646; 31033795}. The cells are also typically negative for uroplakin-3, CDX2, and CK20 (although occasional cases are focally positive for CK20). Expression of these markers, especially if diffuse, should suggest secondary involvement of vulvar skin by urothelial carcinoma or rectal adenocarcinoma {26971063}.

Essential: large epithelial cells with abundant cytoplasm, concentrated in the lower layers of the epidermis but extending upwards, as single cells or small groups of cells, in a pagetoid pattern; these cells express CK7.
The staging of invasive Paget disease is the same as that for other vulvar carcinomas.

Local recurrences are very common, especially, but not exclusively, after incomplete excision, which is common because the Paget cells often extend further than is appreciable clinically (35–60%) {28124023; 29324542; 30458205}. Disease-related mortality is uncommon (< 5%) unless there is invasion {30458205}, but local control can become increasingly difficult with multiple recurrences. Depth of invasion and inguinal lymph node metastasis are associated with increased mortality. The presence of rare isolated tumour cells in the superficial dermis is not associated with a worse prognosis {10542944; 22989161; 23519285; 30458205}. Patients with ERBB2 (HER2)-positive tumours may benefit from targeted treatment if clinically warranted {19519604; 30854041}.
